messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The night Nadia thought she was dying came without warning. She had been healthy her entire life, a thirty-six-year-old construction worker who prided herself on her physical stamina—hauling lumber, operating a jackhammer, keeping pace with men half her age. Then came the chest pain, the crushing pressure that sent her to the emergency room, the diagnosis of a pulmonary embolism that could have killed her within hours. Lying in the hospital bed, she remembered the doctor’s voice as a distant hum; what she remembered most was the certainty that she would never see her husband or her two young children again. She survived, but something in her had not.

In the months that followed, Nadia’s body refused to let her forget. Her sleep fractured: she would jolt awake at 3 a.m., heart hammering, certain she was suffocating. Every creak of the house, every sudden sound on the construction site made her flinch so violently that her coworkers started to notice. “You’re like a cat on a hot roof,” one of them joked, and Nadia forced a laugh, but inside she was terrified. Her body felt like a trap, constantly tense, braced for an attack that never came. She had come to believe that her own reactions meant she was going crazy—that the panic, the hypervigilance, the sleeplessness were proof that something fundamental in her had broken. What frightened her most was the thought that she could not stop bad things from happening; the embolism had come out of nowhere, and if that could happen, then nothing was safe.

To quiet the alarm, Nadia began to work. She volunteered for every overtime shift, took on the heaviest tasks, stayed until the foreman turned off the lights. The exhaustion helped—when she finally collapsed into bed, she was too tired to lie awake for long. But the overworking also fed a darker loop: the more she pushed herself, the more she felt like she was running from something, and that feeling confirmed her sense of helplessness. On her days off, when she could not work, she ate. She would sit in front of the television with a bag of chips or a carton of ice cream, eating mechanically, trying to numb the gnawing dread that lived in her chest. She told herself it was just comfort, but she knew, somewhere underneath, that she was trying to fill a hole that food could not reach. The numbing never lasted; afterward, she felt even more convinced that she was falling apart.

The cycle tightened over weeks and months. The more her body stayed on alert, the more she threw herself into overwork and overeating to escape the feeling—and the more those strategies failed, the more she believed she was losing her mind. Her husband began to complain that she was never home, never present when she was. “You’re like a ghost,” he said one evening, and Nadia could not argue. She had become a ghost to herself.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment on the job site. A forklift backfired, and she dropped to her knees, hands over her head, shaking. The foreman told her to take the rest of the week off. Driving home, Nadia realized she could not keep running. She was terrified that if she stopped working, stopped eating, stopped moving, the fear would swallow her whole—but she was also terrified of what she was becoming. She wanted to feel like herself again, but she no longer knew who that was.
